sandhi.note: a + au → au: इव and औरसान् fuse into इवौरसान्. The final n of पुत्रान् is unchanged before the vowel; the three words are only written together.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (the genitive of the object with an agent noun in -in)
samasa.sense: a group of kings so called; most translators keep it as a name
samasa.alt: It may be a proper name of a people or dynasty (the Kolāvidhvaṃsins) rather than a description. The text uses it again in 1.6 as if a known name, which favours the name; the analysis of the compound is the same either way.

morph.note: Present participle of the curādi stem पालय- (+ śatṛ → पालयत्), genitive singular. With तस्य it gives the circumstance: ‘while he was ruling’. The genitive can be read simply as possessive (‘his enemies’) or as the genitive absolute of disregard (‘though he ruled well, kings became his enemies’); the narrative supports both.
Perfect of √भू, third person plural (-उः). With a predicate nominative, ‘became’: भूपाः शत्रवः बभूवुः ‘kings became (his) enemies’.
Taddhita in -a with vṛddhi of the first syllable: उरस् ‘breast’ → औरस ‘born of the breast’, i.e. a son of one’s own body, as opposed to an adopted son.

mantras.anvaya: प्रजाः औरसान् पुत्रान् इव सम्यक् पालयतः तस्य तदा कोलाविध्वंसिनः भूपाः शत्रवः बभूवुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The genitive phrase (तस्य पालयतः …) frames the clause; the subject is भूपाः with its epithet कोलाविध्वंसिनः, शत्रवः is the predicate, बभूवुः the verb.
mantras.lit: Of him, as he protected his subjects rightly like his own sons, the kings, the Kolāvidhvaṃsins, then became enemies.
mantras.tr: While he ruled his people justly, as though they were his own children, the kings called the Kolāvidhvaṃsins rose against him as enemies.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Rose against him’ renders बभूवुः शत्रवः (‘became enemies’) with the genitive तस्य.

comm.t: The first loss begins. Suratha is a good king — he rules his subjects ‘like his own sons’ — and still enemies arise. The text gives no fault on his side as the cause.
Ruling one’s people as one’s own children is the classical ideal of kingship in the epics and Purāṇas; the verse states it in a single simile and moves on.

flags.uncertain: कोलाविध्वंसिनः: whether a proper name of a people or dynasty or a description (‘destroyers of Kolā’), and what Kolā refers to (a city is often assumed), cannot be settled from the text.

sandhi.note: After a vowel other than a/ā (here ai), the visarga stands as r before a vowel or voiced consonant. The same gives न्यूनैरपि, तैर्युद्धे and कोलाविध्वंसिभिर्जितः.
Final t becomes d before the voiced y; the Gita Press writes the d with virāma and a space.
The visarga of सः is dropped before the consonant t.

samasa.vigraha: अतिप्रबलः दण्डः अतिप्रबलदण्डः; सः अस्य अस्ति इति अतिप्रबलदण्डी, तस्य
samasa.type: karmadhāraya (अतिप्रबलदण्ड) with the possessive taddhita -in; अतिप्रबल is itself a prādi tatpuruṣa (अतिशयेन प्रबलः)
samasa.sense: a king whose army and power of punishment were very great
samasa.alt: दण्ड can mean the army or the king’s power to punish (daṇḍanīti); both fit, and the contrast with न्यूनैः (‘weaker’) favours military strength.

morph.note: Past passive participle of √जि with the auxiliary ‘was’ understood: सः … जितः ‘he (was) defeated’. The agent is in the instrumental (कोलाविध्वंसिभिः).
Imperfect of √भू with augment a-: ‘(a battle) took place’. The narrative moves between imperfect, aorist and perfect without difference of sense.

mantras.anvaya: अतिप्रबलदण्डिनः तस्य तैः युद्धम् अभवत्। न्यूनैः अपि तैः कोलाविध्वंसिभिः सः युद्धे जितः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two sentences: a battle took place (युद्धम् अभवत्); he was defeated (सः जितः), with the agent and its concessive qualifier न्यूनैः अपि.
mantras.lit: A battle took place between him, who had a very strong force, and them; even though they were weaker, he was defeated in battle by those Kolāvidhvaṃsins.
mantras.tr: War broke out between them and the king, mighty as his forces were; and though they were the weaker side, the Kolāvidhvaṃsins defeated him in battle.

comm.t: The paradox is in अपि: the strong king loses to the weaker side. The verse does not explain it; the following verses show his own ministers turning against him.
A modern reading: strength on paper does not decide the outcome. The story strips Suratha of power that was never as secure as it looked.

sandhi.note: -aḥ before a- becomes -o, and the following a is absorbed (avagraha). Inside the compound, देश + अधिप → देशाधिप by अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः (6.1.101).
सः loses its visarga before m; महाभागः and तैः each turn their visarga to s before t.

samasa.alt: Also analysed as a karmadhāraya, स्वं च तत् पुरं च, ‘his own city’; the sense is the same.

samasa.sense: the universal king of 1.4 is now master only of his home territory

morph.note: With verbs of motion the kta participle is active: आयातः ‘(he) having come’, not ‘having been reached’. Its goal stands in the accusative (स्वपुरम्).
Here the kta is passive, with the agent in the instrumental (तैः … प्रबलारिभिः): ‘he was overrun by them’.

mantras.anvaya: ततः स्वपुरम् आयातः (सः) निजदेशाधिपः अभवत्। तदा सः महाभागः तैः प्रबलारिभिः आक्रान्तः।
mantras.anvaya_en: First sentence: participle + predicate nominative + verb. Second: passive participle as verb with an instrumental agent.
mantras.lit: Then, having come to his own city, he became ruler of his own country; then that illustrious one was attacked by them, the powerful enemies.
mantras.tr: Then he withdrew to his own city and ruled only his own land; and even there that noble king was assailed by those enemies, now grown strong.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Only’ and ‘even there’ make explicit the contrast with 1.4 (‘over the whole earth’), which the compound निजदेशाधिपः implies.

comm.t: The second loss: the emperor of 1.4 is reduced to his home territory, and the enemies follow him there.
The steps of Suratha’s fall — empire, country, city, treasury, army — are told in order, so that by 1.9 nothing royal is left to him but the name महाभाग.

sandhi.note: After ai and i the visarga stands as r before the voiced b and d: three junctions in a row, which give the line its rolling sound.
a + a → ā. The final m of अपहृतम् becomes anusvāra before t (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

samasa.literal: of one whose strength is poor
by those whose selves are bad

morph.note: Passive participle as verb, neuter singular although it has a masculine (कोशः) and a neuter (बलम्) subject: it agrees with the nearer one, बलम्, or takes the neuter for a mixed pair. ‘The treasury and the army were seized.’
Instrumental plural of बलिन्, an -in stem (बल + possessive -in): ‘having strength’. Contrast दुर्बलस्य in the same line: the ministers are strong, the king weak.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तत्र स्वपुरे अपि बलिभिः दुष्टैः दुरात्मभिः अमात्यैः दुर्बलस्य (तस्य) कोशः बलं च अपहृतम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The passive participle अपहृतम् is the verb; its subjects are कोशः बलं च, its agent the ministers with three adjectives, and दुर्बलस्य names whose treasury.
mantras.lit: Then, even there in his own city, the treasury and the army of the weakened one were carried off by his powerful, corrupt, evil-minded ministers.
mantras.tr: Then, in his own city too, his powerful ministers — corrupt and wicked men — seized the weakened king’s treasury and army.

comm.t: The third loss comes from inside: his own ministers take the treasury (कोश) and the army (बल), the two supports of kingship. The king is now called दुर्बल ‘weak’, the ministers बलिन् ‘strong’.
Treasury and army are two of the classical ‘limbs’ of the state (rājyāṅga); Suratha will speak of his attachment to the limbs of his kingdom in 1.41.

samasa.literal: by the pretext of the hunt
samasa.sense: on the excuse of going hunting

samasa.literal: one whose lordship has been taken

samasa.sense: king — said with irony of a king who has lost his land

morph.note: Absolutive with a prefix, so -य (lyap) instead of -त्वा: आ + √रुह् + ल्यप् → आरुह्य ‘having mounted’. Its subject is the subject of the main verb जगाम.
Nominative singular of एकाकिन् ‘solitary’ (एक + -आकिन्); n-stems in -in lose the n in the nominative and lengthen the i.
Perfect of √गम्, with reduplication ज- (g → j) and vṛddhi of the root vowel in the third singular.

mantras.anvaya: ततः हृतस्वाम्यः सः भूपतिः मृगयाव्याजेन एकाकी हयम् आरुह्य गहनं वनं जगाम।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with its bahuvrīhi epithet, the manner (मृगयाव्याजेन, एकाकी), the absolutive with its object, then the main verb with its goal.
mantras.lit: Then that king, robbed of his sovereignty, on the pretext of hunting, alone, having mounted a horse, went to a dense forest.
mantras.tr: Stripped of his kingdom, the king rode out alone on horseback under the pretext of a hunt, and went into a deep forest.

comm.t: The last step: the king leaves alone, keeping up appearances (‘as if to hunt’). The forest is where the story can turn.
A modern reading: the pretext matters. Even in defeat Suratha is guarding how he is seen — the attachment to position that he will confess in 1.12–16.
